options.counterfactual: The set \(\mathcal G\) need not contain its positive supremum; passing to a quasitracial ultraproduct can destroy a necessary hypothesis of the proposed endpoint construction.
options.approach: Audit the ultraproduct construction axiom by axiom, especially whether the limiting quasitrace is linear on every abelian subalgebra when commuting elements need not have commuting representatives.

options.counterfactual: The set \(\mathcal G\) is nonempty, but its supremum is strictly less than \(\tfrac12\), so none of the three proposed answers is correct.
options.approach: Search for a stronger universal upper bound using three or more increments and the matrix extension of the quasitrace, rather than the two-increment argument yielding \(\eta\le\tfrac12\).

options.approach: Investigate corner restriction and normalization of bounded positive partial sums. Determine whether these operations have an invariant that could prevent amplification beyond a threshold below \(\tfrac12\).

options.counterfactual: Every faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace on a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor sends the terms of a positive series with bounded partial sums to zero, and consequently \(\mathcal G=\varnothing\).
options.approach: Revisit the projection reduction and seek an independently justified theorem excluding infinitely many projections of uniformly positive dimension with bounded partial sums. Do not assume that projection-lattice finiteness alone proves it.

options.approach: Investigate whether a quasitrace has sufficient sequential order continuity in a suitable completion to force the increment values to vanish, without requiring that the supremum belong to the original algebra.

options.counterfactual: Every faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace on a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor sends the terms of a positive series with bounded partial sums to zero, and consequently \(\mathcal G=\varnothing\).
options.approach: Search for a quantitative inequality controlling positive increments by changes in quasitrace values or spectral distributions. Check whether such an inequality would inadvertently imply general quasitrace additivity before relying on it.
